lesson.title: Anaphase: Sister Chromatids Go Their Separate Ways
lesson.summary: Anaphase is the stage of mitosis when sister chromatids finally separate and are pulled to opposite poles of the cell, each becoming its own independent chromosome.
lesson.body:
Anaphase is the moment mitosis has been building toward: the physical separation of sister chromatids. It begins when the cohesin proteins holding each chromosome's two sister chromatids together at the centromere are cleaved by an enzyme called separase. The instant that connection is cut, the two sister chromatids are no longer physically linked, and each is now considered a complete, independent chromosome in its own right. The spindle microtubules attached to their kinetochores, which had been holding the chromatids in place at the metaphase plate, immediately begin shortening, reeling each newly independent chromosome toward the spindle pole it is attached to.

While the kinetochore microtubules are pulling chromosomes poleward, a second set of spindle microtubules, ones that overlap in the middle of the cell rather than attaching to chromosomes, slide past each other and push the two poles further apart, elongating the whole cell. This elongation, together with the chromosome movement, is what gives anaphase its visibly dramatic appearance under a microscope: two clusters of chromosomes rushing toward opposite ends of a cell that is itself stretching lengthwise. This is also when the machinery for the next step starts staging, as microfilaments begin organizing at the cell's midline in preparation for the contractile ring that will carry out cytokinesis once mitosis finishes.

Getting anaphase right matters enormously, because this is the one point in the entire cycle where genetic material is physically and irreversibly divided. If a chromosome fails to separate properly, an error called nondisjunction, one daughter cell can end up with an extra chromosome and the other with one too few, a condition called aneuploidy that can be lethal to the resulting cells or cause serious developmental problems. That is exactly the kind of error the spindle assembly checkpoint in metaphase exists to prevent, by making sure every chromosome is correctly attached before anaphase is allowed to begin at all.
